conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for new mothers during the weeks and months after birth, when emotions can swing so wildly and everything can feel overwhelming.

In front of us is the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It isn’t a pass-or-fail test; it’s simply a way for us to check in on your mood, anxiety, and overall well-being so we know what kind of support might help you feel more like yourself again.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within our treatment team, and you can take your time with each question. There are just ten items, and I’ll read each one aloud so we can talk through your answer together. If any question feels difficult, we can pause, breathe, and move forward when you’re ready.

Shall we begin?  
Here’s the first question:  

Over the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[slow inhale, eyes on the blanket in my lap]  
Honestly… not very often. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute video or if my mom makes a silly face at the baby, but it’s like the laugh gets stuck—like I hear myself make the sound, yet I don’t feel it inside the way I used to. Maybe once or twice this week I’ve actually giggled, but it fades fast and I’m right back to this heavy, empty feeling.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[quiet voice, eyes still lowered]  
I’d say… “not so often.” I can still laugh a little if something’s really funny, but it’s like I’m faking it most of the time. The joy just doesn’t feel real or last long before the sadness comes back.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugging slightly, pulling the blanket tighter]  
Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a new show to binge—but now it all feels… flat. I still go through the motions, hoping maybe I’ll feel something, but mostly I’m just tired and counting the hours until bedtime.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes flick up, then back down]  
Yeah… more than I’d like to admit. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong.” Even tiny stuff—like forgetting a burp cloth—turns into “I’m a terrible mom.” I know it’s not logical, but the thought just barges in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping the blanket tighter around my shoulders]  
Pretty much every day. My mind keeps circling—Is the baby breathing? Did I fasten the car seat right? What if I drop her? There’s no real reason, but the worry just sits on my chest and won’t move. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but it pops right back up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]  
Yes… a couple of times. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air, like something awful is about to happen even when everything’s quiet. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment I’m sure I’m losing control.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly, eyes fixed on my clasped hands]  
Most days, yeah. It’s like I’m drowning in small tasks—changing a diaper, answering a text, folding one onesie—and they all feel huge. I’ll look at the pile of laundry and just freeze, thinking, “I can’t do this.” I still get through it, but it’s like wading through thick mud every step.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet, rubbing the edge of the blanket]  
Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t settle. I replay everything I might’ve done wrong with the baby, or I picture scary “what-ifs,” and then I’m wide awake. It usually takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and when I finally drift off I wake up again with my heart pounding. It’s been that way three or four nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

[soft voice, eyes glassy]  
Yeah… pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears coming for no clear reason. I wouldn’t say I’m crying all day, but that sad, heavy feeling is there more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallowing hard, nodding]  
Yes… twice this week it got that bad. Once was in the shower—everyone else asleep, hot water running, and I just slid down the tile and sobbed. The second time the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt useless; I ended up crying into her blanket while she napped. It felt like the sadness had to spill out somewhere.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice barely above a whisper]  
Once or twice… it’s more like a flash than a real plan. I’ll be rocking her at 3 a.m. and think, “What if I just disappeared?” or picture driving into the guardrail on the way to the pediatrician. I don’t want to die—I just want the ache to stop. I haven’t told anyone; I’m scared they’ll take the baby away.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: SCREENING NOTE – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety Screen  

Symptoms/Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked guilt/self-blame (“bad mom” cognitions)  
- Chronic, intrusive worry and two recent panic spells  
- Overwhelm by routine infant-care tasks; describes “drowning”  
- Initial insomnia with mid-night re-awakenings 3-4×/wk  
- Passive suicidal ideation (twice this week): “I just want the ache to stop;” no active plan, states does not want to die  

Observed Patterns  
- Consistent dysphoria across all functional domains (sleep, pleasure, coping)  
- Anxiety symptoms equally prominent and not situation-specific  
- Cognitive distortions center on maternal competence and infant safety  
- Emotional disclosure accompanied by psychomotor slowing, avoidant eye contact, self-soothing behaviors (blanket wrapping)  

Screening Significance  
- Meets clinical threshold for further evaluation of Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety  
- Safety concern: presence of self-harm ideation with specific imagery (driving into guardrail) though denied intent; protective factors (bond with infant, fear of infant removal)  

Risk Factors  
- First 12 weeks postpartum, sleep deprivation, self-reported social silence regarding thoughts  

Next Step  
- Refer immediately for comprehensive psychiatric assessment; consider same-day safety planning and development of support/supervision plan for mother and infant.
